entities.summary:
The Gospel of Judas is a non-canonical Christian religious text that has garnered significant scholarly attention due to its unique narrative and historical context. Composed in the 2nd century AD, this Coptic manuscript contains conversations between Jesus and his disciples, particularly Judas Iscariot, which offers an alternative perspective on the betrayal of Jesus.

The Gospel of Judas was written during a period of significant religious and cultural upheaval in the Mediterranean world. The text's existence has been confirmed through multiple independent sources, including the discovery of a Coptic manuscript fragment in 1978. The manuscript has since been extensively studied, with many scholars arguing that it provides valuable insights into the early Christian community and its relationships with other Jewish groups.

Despite its significance, the Gospel of Judas is not without controversy. Some scholars have questioned the text's authenticity, while others have raised concerns about its potential influence on the development of Christian theology. Nevertheless, the Gospel of Judas remains an important historical document that continues to be studied and debated by scholars today.

The legacy of the Gospel of Judas can be seen in its influence on later Christian texts, such as the Gnostic writings of the Nag Hammadi library. The manuscript's focus on the role of Judas Iscariot has also led to a reevaluation of his character and significance within Christian tradition.

In conclusion, the Gospel of Judas is a significant historical document that offers valuable insights into the early Christian community and its relationships with other Jewish groups. Its legacy can be seen in later Christian texts and continues to be studied and debated by scholars today.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Gospel of Judas is a Gnostic text purporting to record secret conversations between Jesus and Judas Iscariot in the days before the Crucifixion, known to exist from the church father Irenaeus of Lyon's criticism of it c. 180 CE but lost until a fragmentary Coptic manuscript (Codex Tchacos) was discovered in Egypt c. 1970 and eventually published by National Geographic in April 2006 following its conservation and scholarly analysis. The text presents Judas not as the betrayer of Jesus but as his most favoured disciple — the only apostle who truly understands Jesus's cosmic mission — and his 'betrayal' is reinterpreted as fulfilling Jesus's own instruction: 'You will sacrifice the man who clothes me' (referring to Jesus's physical body), enabling the liberation of Jesus's divine spirit from its material imprisonment.

The Gospel of Judas represents one of the most radical revisions of the canonical passion narrative in Gnostic Christianity — its theological framework is dualistic, viewing the material world as the creation of a lower, ignorant deity (the Demiurge) and the physical body as a prison for the divine spark within. In this framework, death is liberation and the Crucifixion is a positive event enabling the escape of Jesus's divine spirit from bodily imprisonment. The canonical Judas — the quintessential betrayer, whose name became synonymous with treachery in Western culture — is transformed into a heroic, enlightened disciple acting at his master's instruction.

The Gospel of Judas's 2006 publication generated enormous public interest and media coverage — it was presented as a potentially revolutionary revision of Christian origins that would force a reassessment of Judas's role in the Passion narrative.
